L390: ### The Look and Feel of the Original
L391: 
L392: Experience the classic Atari 8-bit computer, now with HDMI output, 25 built-in games, and other modern updates. The 800XL retains the look and feel of the original, including a full-sized mechanical keyboard, baked in Atari BASIC, and a working cartridge slot, while adding features designed for modern displays and gaming setups.
L393: 
L394: 【76†Image: Complete with THECXSTICK】
L395: ### Complete with THECXSTICK
L396: 
L397: Includes updated THECXSTICK, a modern recreation of the joystick with eight buttons. Connect additional controllers and USB storage devices via four USB-A ports.
L398: 
L399: 【77†Image: Working Cartridge Slot】
L400: ### Working Cartridge Slot
L401: 
L402: The cartridge slot supports most Atari 400, 800, XL, and XE cartridges. Also features support for software created for 8-bit computers and the Atari 5200 console. Load your own games and software from USB flash drives with cartridge, disk and cassette image support.

L143: Chapter 9
L144: The PlayStation
L145: ## Part 1 Ohga's Decision: "Do it!"
L146: The video game market throughout much of the 1980s was dominated by Nintendo's Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), and after news of Nintendo starting development on the next-generation Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) reached the ears of Sony, discussions arose concerning a potential technological collaboration between the two companies.
L147: Although Sony had not expanded into the video game market yet, the possibility of using the Sony-developed CD-ROM in place of the ROM cartridges used in the industry up until that point gave the two companies the chance to create a truly new type of gaming console.
L148: Thus, a contract was finalized in early 1990 on the joint development of what would later be referred to as the Super NES CD-ROM, a fully integrated CD-ROM gaming console, between Sony and Nintendo. This proposed console was tentatively named the "PlayStation," though the collaboration ultimately never came to fruition. Yet despite the project going up in smoke, project leader Ken Kutaragi strongly believed that Sony needed to continue development independently on a CD-ROM-based console.
L149: Looking towards the future, he knew that Sony could not afford to give up on this new business venture.
L150: The project's cancellation nevertheless fueled sentiments within the company that Sony should withdraw from video games altogether, but a turning point came in 1992 during a mid-year management meeting. Questioned on his project team's future direction, Kutaragi spoke candidly and insistently: "Sony must pursue the creation of its own game console and format.
L151: Separate from the collaboration with Nintendo, we've actually been independently developing our own original three-dimensional computer graphics (3D-CG) system in secret. With this technology, we'll be able to render 3D images that would blow the SNES out of the water." Clearly seeing Kutaragi's ardor for the project, Ohga responded, "if that's what you're claiming, then prove it!" Then, slamming his fist down on the table, he shouted in English that fateful command at Kutaragi: "Do it!"
L152: This moment marked the instant that Sony's video game business would start to take off.
L153: ## Part 2 Founding Sony Computer Entertainment (SCE)
L154: 
L155: 【55†Image】
L156: 
L157: The PlayStation Prototype Demo Event (1994)
L158: 
L159: 【56†Image】
L160: 
L161: Ohga's Speech at the Third-Party Developer Seminar (1993)
L162: The name "PlayStation" for Sony's new gaming platform was chosen to contrast with the word "workstation," differentiating "computers for work" and "computers for play." Concerning the novel combination of computers and entertainment with 3D-CG, Kutaragi himself explained that "we really wanted to make a computer meant solely for entertainment and create the wholly new and unprecedented market of 'computer entertainment.'"
L163: As the development team around Kutaragi prepared to start work on the project in earnest, they set up the "Computer Entertainment Business Preparations Room" in the Shin Aoyama building in Tokyo's Aoyama neighborhood. Engineers from Sony came to join the project, as well as Epic/Sony founder Shigeo Maruyama from Sony Music Entertainment (SMEJ).
L164: One significant barrier had to be overcome at the very start, however. Since Sony didn't have any video game software titles of its own, creating these titles for the PlayStation would have to be left to third-party developers. In stark contrast to its competitors who already had an established catalogue of titles, the PlayStation was incapable of launching a whole new format on its own.
L165: At the project's outset, both Kutaragi and Maruyama traveled all across the country to negotiate with various developers, but responses were far from enthusiastic. If anything, their words were more often met with disbelieving looks, clearly reflecting doubts that what they were proposing was even possible in the first place.
L166: This all changed in October 1993.
L167: As a joint venture between Sony and Sony Music Entertainment (SMEJ), the two companies announced on October 27 that they would together launch a new company, Sony Computer Entertainment (SCE), in November of that year. The new company would develop and sell both home video game consoles and its respective software, while also managing licenses with external developers.

L37: Xbox Live Sets New Online Gaming Benchmark
L38: Xbox Popularity Rises With Steady Market Share Growth in 2004
L39: REDMOND, Wash. ?” Jan. 20, 2005 ?” Coming off one of the hottest holiday seasons for video game software sales in history, Microsoft Corp. today announced that its Xbox Live” online gaming service has set a new standard with more than 1.4 million members, exceeding expectations and cementing its leadership position in the digital entertainment landscape.
L40: This additional news comes on the heels of 14 consecutive months of increased market share for Xbox, the only console to see an increase of market share in 2004.
L41: ?oOur consumers are passionate about online gameplay and seek larger-than-life digital entertainment experiences,? said Robbie Bach, senior vice president of the Home and Entertainment Division and chief Xbox officer at Microsoft. ?oWe will continue to offer our thriving community best-in-class games, downloadable content, unique programming, and the expanded features and services found only on Xbox and Xbox Live.?
L42: The success of Xbox Live reinforces a stellar holiday season for the Xbox platform, which saw Xbox lead competitors in consoles sales, according to recently released data from NPD Funworld.* Other highlights from NPD Funworld include these:
L43: 
L44: ? Monthly share for Xbox has grown year-to-year every month for 14 consecutive months, climbing 11 share points to 37 percent in December.
L45: ? Xbox was the only platform to see year-to-year growth during the fourth quarter of 2004 and the full calendar year 2004, while Xbox competitors and the overall market declined year over year for both time periods.
L46: 
L47: ? Xbox annual 2004 console unit market share increased an impressive 12 points compared with 2003 and ended the year with a 37 percent share.
L48: ? Xbox had three titles in the top 10 in December: No. 4, ?oHalo 2? from Microsoft Games Studios (including sales of the Limited Edition); No. 6, ?oNeed for Speed: Underground 2? from Electronic Arts Inc.; and No. 10, ?oStar Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 2? from LucasArts.
L49: 
L50: ? Xbox software sales led the way in 2004 as unit sales increased 46 percent year-over-year, and increased 55 percent (annual 2004 vs. annual 2003).
L51: There are now more than 200 Xbox Live-enabled titles, making it the richest library of online console games available today. ?oHalo 2,? which has sold more than 6.4 million copies worldwide since November, helped propel the service to new heights. The overall ?oHalo? franchise, which includes predecessor ?oHalo: Combat Evolved? for the PC and Xbox, has sold a collective 12.8 million copies in just three years.
L52: The ?oHalo 2? sell-through in the United States is just shy of 4.4 million units in less than two months.**
L53: ?oThe Xbox Live community has an insatiable appetite for riveting, connected and social game experiences,? said Cameron Ferroni, general manager of Xbox Live. ?oOur ongoing vision is to create online experiences that top anything else our community has seen to date. ?~Halo 2′ is another great example of how Xbox Live continues to set the standard for online gameplay.?
L54: Smashing previously established records, the Xbox Live community has logged a record-breaking 91 million hours playing ?oHalo 2? since the title’s launch ?” more than any other Xbox Live game in the two-year history of the service. In addition, the instantly immersive gameplay has resulted in close to 61 million logged sessions on the game, with an average session lasting nearly 92 minutes, approximately the length of a major motion picture.
L55: Blockbuster Xbox Live-enabled titles in 2005 promise to boost additional Xbox Live membership growth. Games such as Microsoft Game Studios’ ?oForza Motorsport”,? LucasArts’ ?oStar Wars Republic Commando,? Vicarious Visions’ ?oDoom 3? and Rare’s ?oConker”: Live and Reloaded? promise to drive additional online gaming growth in the coming months.
L56: In addition, Xbox Live members now can enjoy Xbox Live Arcade, a new social experience that brings popular retro classics and broad-appeal games directly to the Xbox console over the Xbox Live service. Members now have a personal arcade connected to Xbox Live, offering quick and easy access to classic arcade games such as ?oMs.
L57: Pac-Man? and ?oDig Dug? as well as exciting new games such as ?oBejeweled? and ?oAlien Sky.? From late-night gamers to those looking for a quick five-minute game fix between ?oHalo 2? matches, Xbox Live Arcade has something for everyone in the household.
L58: Microsoft introduced the first broadly adopted online gaming service in November 2002 and continues to expand the appeal and adoption of broadband. The service continues to evolve with improved features such as downloadable content, voice messages and alerts coupled with highly anticipated games and unique programming such as ?oGame with Fame,? ?oPlay and Win? and ?oMystery Gamer.?
